english: Let $f:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function, differentiable at $x=1$, such that $f(xy)=f(x)+f(y)$ for all $x,y\in(0,\infty)$ and $f'(1)=2$. Let $h:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined by $h(x)=x^{2}-3x+f(x)$. Then which of the following statements is TRUE?
(A) $h$ is a bijection, and the equation $h(x)=h^{-1}(x)$ has exactly one solution, which lies in the interval $(3,4)$
(B) $h$ is a bijection, and the equation $h(x)=h^{-1}(x)$ has exactly one solution, namely $x=1$
(C) $h$ is a bijection, and the equation $h(x)=h^{-1}(x)$ has exactly three solutions
hindi: माना कि $f:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ एक फलन है, जो $x=1$ पर अवकलनीय है, तथा सभी $x,y\in(0,\infty)$ के लिए $f(xy)=f(x)+f(y)$ एवं $f'(1)=2$ है। माना कि $h:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$, $h(x)=x^{2}-3x+f(x)$ द्वारा परिभाषित है। तब निम्न में से कौन-सा कथन सत्य है?
(A) $h$ एकैकी तथा आच्छादक है, और समीकरण $h(x)=h^{-1}(x)$ का ठीक एक हल है, जो अन्तराल $(3,4)$ में स्थित है
(B) $h$ एकैकी तथा आच्छादक है, और समीकरण $h(x)=h^{-1}(x)$ का ठीक एक हल है, अर्थात् $x=1$
(C) $h$ एकैकी तथा आच्छादक है, और समीकरण $h(x)=h^{-1}(x)$ के ठीक तीन हल हैं
solution: $h'(x)=2x-3+\dfrac2x=\dfrac{2x^{2}-3x+2}{x}>0$ (discriminant $9-16<0$), so $h$ is strictly increasing, hence one-one; $h\to-\infty$ as $x\to0^{+}$ and $h\to\infty$ as $x\to\infty$, so $h$ is onto $\mathbb{R}$
For increasing $h$: if $h(x)=h^{-1}(x)=y$ then $h(y)=x$; $x<y\Rightarrow h(x)<h(y)$, i.e. $y<x$, contradiction (similarly $x>y$). So $h(x)=h^{-1}(x)\iff h(x)=x$ (graphs meet only on $y=x$)
$g(x)=h(x)-x=x^{2}-4x+2\log_e x$, $g'(x)=\dfrac{2(x-1)^{2}}{x}\ge0$: $g$ strictly increasing, at most one root
$g(3)=2\log_e3-3<0$, $g(4)=2\log_e4>0$: exactly one root, in $(3,4)$ ($g(1)=-3\ne0$, so (B) is wrong)
solution_full: Putting $x=y=1$: $f(1)=2f(1)$, so $f(1)=0$. For $x>0$ and small $t$: $f(x+t)=f\left(x\left(1+\dfrac tx\right)\right)=f(x)+f\left(1+\dfrac tx\right)$.

Hence $\dfrac{f(x+t)-f(x)}{t}=\dfrac1x\cdot\dfrac{f\left(1+\frac tx\right)-f(1)}{t/x}\to\dfrac{f'(1)}{x}=\dfrac2x$ as $t\to0$. So $f$ is differentiable on $(0,\infty)$ with $f'(x)=\dfrac2x$, and with $f(1)=0$ this gives $f(x)=2\log_e x$.

Then $h(x)=x^{2}-3x+2\log_e x$ and $h'(x)=2x-3+\dfrac2x=\dfrac{2x^{2}-3x+2}{x}$. The quadratic $2x^{2}-3x+2$ has discriminant $9-16<0$ and positive leading coefficient, so $h'(x)>0$ on $(0,\infty)$: $h$ is strictly increasing and therefore one-one, so (D) is wrong.

As $x\to0^{+}$, $2\log_e x\to-\infty$ while $x^{2}-3x\to0$, so $h(x)\to-\infty$; as $x\to\infty$, $h(x)\to\infty$. Being continuous, $h$ takes every real value: $h$ is a bijection from $(0,\infty)$ onto $\mathbb{R}$ and $h^{-1}:\mathbb{R}\to(0,\infty)$ exists.

Let $x>0$ satisfy $h(x)=h^{-1}(x)$ and put $y=h(x)$; then $y>0$ and $h(y)=x$. If $x<y$, monotonicity gives $h(x)<h(y)$, i.e. $y<x$, a contradiction; if $x>y$ we get $y>x$, again a contradiction. So $y=x$. Conversely $h(x)=x$ gives $h^{-1}(x)=x=h(x)$. Thus the equation is equivalent to $h(x)=x$: the graph of an increasing function meets its mirror image in $y=x$ only on that line.
Let $g(x)=h(x)-x=x^{2}-4x+2\log_e x$. Then $g'(x)=2x-4+\dfrac2x=\dfrac{2(x-1)^{2}}{x}\ge0$, with equality only at $x=1$, so $g$ is strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$ and has at most one zero.
$g(3)=9-12+2\log_e3=2\log_e3-3<0$ since $\log_e3<1.5$, and $g(4)=16-16+2\log_e4>0$. By the intermediate value theorem $g$ has exactly one zero, lying in $(3,4)$ (numerically $x\approx3.28$).

So $h(x)=h^{-1}(x)$ has exactly one solution, in $(3,4)$: (A) is true. $g(1)=-3\ne0$, so (B) is wrong, and three solutions (as can happen for a decreasing function) is impossible here, so (C) is wrong.
originality_note: New: a logarithmic Cauchy equation produces h(x)=x^2-3x+2 ln x, whose monotonicity (a negative discriminant) gives the inverse, and then h=h^{-1} is reduced to h(x)=x, located by IVT (way 5). Closest known: (1/16)^x = log_{1/16} x (decreasing case, three solutions) and f=f^{-1} for an increasing cubic. Different because: f must first be recovered from the equation, and the root has no closed form, so the student must prove uniqueness and locate it.

concept_use.Cauchy’s Functional Equations: Standard: f(xy)=f(x)+f(y) with f'(1)=2 is solved to give f(x)=2 ln x.
concept_use.One-one vs many-one: monotonicity, horiz: h'(x)=(2x^2-3x+2)/x>0 shows h is strictly increasing, hence one-one (statement D is wrong).
concept_use.Inverse of a function: existence, graph: h is a continuous increasing map of (0,inf) onto R, so h^{-1} exists, and its graph is the mirror image of h in y=x.
concept_use.Solving f(x) = f_inv(x): For increasing h, h(x)=h^{-1}(x) is shown equivalent to h(x)=x, whose unique root in (3,4) is found by monotonicity of g and IVT.

stem_review: Read as a student: f's domain, the equation, differentiability only at 1 and f'(1)=2 stated; h defined with domain and codomain. The four options are all statements about h, exactly (A) true (root about 3.2756, checked numerically, and a scan of h(h(t))=t found one sign change only). Changed: No change.
key_step: For strictly increasing h, h(x)=h^{-1}(x) reduces to h(x)=x; then g=x^2-4x+2 ln x is increasing with g(3)<0<g(4).
justification: Several linked ideas: solving the Cauchy equation from differentiability at one point, a monotonicity check for invertibility, the increasing-function reduction to y=x, and IVT. Each is standard, the chain is genuine. Comparable to 2026-P1-Q1 (L3, sign of f' via an auxiliary function) and 2024-P2-Q10 (L1, monotone root count).
blueprint_concepts: Cauchy’s Functional Equations: Standard forms like f(x+y)=f(x)f(y), f(xy)=f(x)+f(y)
One-one vs many-one: monotonicity, horizontal line and algebraic tests
Inverse of a function: existence, graph symmetry about y = x
